name: Chest binder

image.caption: Chest binders in various skin tones DSCF2250

lead: A chest binder is a tight, usually spandex or nylon garment worn over the torso to compress breast tissue so the chest looks flatter under clothing. Transgender men, nonbinary people and others use it to get a flatter, more masculine silhouette; cisgender men with gynecomastia, performers, cosplayers and people recovering from surgery also use compression garments.

The effect lasts only while it is worn. Surveys of users report that many feel binding helps them express their gender, and many also report physical effects such as back pain, shortness of breath, overheating and skin irritation [1][2]. Studies are mostly surveys and small pilot studies, and no standardized binding guidelines exist [2].

paras: Commercial binders come as short tank styles, half-length tops and wraps in a range of compression levels. Some people instead use high-compression sports bras or layered clothing, which a study cited on Wikipedia found caused the fewest physical problems. Community and clinical guidance commonly discusses fewer binding days per week and size fit; a 2024 survey link between more days of binding and more complications is described in the literature [1].

Reported effects include back and chest pain, shortness of breath, overheating, itching and rashes, and, more rarely, rib problems and changes in breast tissue [1]. A case report described prolonged oxygen desaturation in a patient who wore a binder under anesthesia [3]. Elastic bandages, duct tape and plastic wrap are described as higher-risk improvisations [1]. In December 2025 the FDA sent warning letters to binder sellers about device registration [4].

More masculine or androgynous torso profile
angle.text: A binder compresses the chest so shirts hang flatter, giving a more masculine or androgynous profile while it is worn. People also wear compression garments over gynecomastia or after surgery for a smoother contour.

lead: A chest binder is a compression garment, typically spandex or nylon, worn to flatten the appearance of the chest under clothing. People use binders to give the torso a flatter, more masculine or androgynous profile. Transgender men and nonbinary people are the main users and often bind to ease gender dysphoria or while awaiting surgery; others bind for gynecomastia, costuming, sports, or comfort after surgery or injury [1].

The appearance effect is immediate and temporary, ending when the garment is removed. Commercial binders have been sold online and in stores for up to roughly $30 as of 2024, and the main alternatives are high-compression sports bras, athletic compression wear and layered clothing [1].

Research consists chiefly of community surveys, small physiological studies and case reports. A 2020 survey of US trans and nonbinary adults found 92% felt binding helped them express their gender, and many reported physical discomfort [1]. In December 2025 the US FDA sent warning letters to companies selling binders, treating them as medical devices that had not been registered and listed [2].
infobox: Spandex, nylon; also tape and wraps (higher risk)

Moxiong and dudou in imperial China; flapper-era flattening in the 1920s [1]

paras: Commercial binders include wraps, undershirt-style tanks and sports-bra-like designs, usually in spandex or nylon. Community groups often regard them as the safest option, although one study linked them to some of the most negative physical effects [1]. Sports bras and layered clothing are alternatives, and tape designed for binding exists. Household improvisations such as elastic bandages, duct tape and plastic wrap are described as high-risk [1].

Breast flattening garments appear in several cultures: the moxiong and dudou were popular in Tang and Song dynasty China, binding persisted among upper-class Chinese women until the 1930s, Korean hanbok and Japanese kimono styles flattened the bust, and some Catholic nuns bound until the early 20th century [1]. In the 1920s flapper fashion favoured a flat-chested look and many women bound [1]. Modern binders for gender expression are sold by trans-focused apparel companies and community organisations, and one such group, Point of Pride, reported around 40 requests a day in 2026 [1].

Transgender men and nonbinary people bind to reduce dysphoria, to feel gender euphoria, or to bridge the wait for surgery. Others bind for recovery after surgery, lactation suppression, costuming, sports, feeling safer in public, or gynecomastia [1]. An Australian study in 2015 found 87% of transmasculine respondents had bound [1], and a 2020 to 2021 youth study of 13 to 24 year olds found 89% had tried binding [1].

A 2024 community-informed cross-sectional survey of transgender and nonbinary users of commercial and non-commercial binders noted that no standardized binding guidelines exist for clinicians and aimed to show the need for evidence on binder type and health outcomes [3].

A 2025 pilot study of 18 transgender and gender diverse youth assigned female at birth, mean age 14.9, compared exercise testing with and without a commercial binder and found no significant differences in cardiopulmonary exercise parameters; spirometry data were insufficient to compare [4]. A case report described prolonged oxygen desaturation in a 19-year-old transgender man who wore a binder during anesthesia, with authors recommending that clinicians ask patients about binding before procedures [5].
Related surgical research includes a retrospective study of ultrasound-assisted liposuction for top surgery in transgender men that measured satisfaction and quality of life [6].

Surveys report back pain, shortness of breath, overheating, poor posture, skin rashes and yeast infections beneath the breasts. Rarer reports include rib fractures, permanent breast deformation, scarring and reduced skin elasticity that may affect later chest surgery [1]. Some survey findings link complications more to the number of days per week of binding than to hours per session, and binding is also associated in a 2024 survey with lower anxiety and dysphoria [1]. Duct tape and plastic wrap are described as especially dangerous [1].

On 16 December 2025 the FDA issued warning letters to companies selling breast binders, including one to ShapeShifter Apparel. The agency said website statements linking binders to gender dysphoria show the products are intended to affect the body's structure or function and so qualify as medical devices, that custom-made claims amount to manufacturing, and that the firm had not registered or listed the devices for fiscal year 2026, making them misbranded [2]. The letter requested a response within fifteen business days and noted possible seizure or injunction. Advocacy outlets criticised the action and described binders as previously unregulated, while the agency framed it as a registration matter [2][1].
